excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: In plane geometry each figure is restricted so that all of its parts lie in the same plane. Such figures are called \emph{two-dimensional figures}.
excerpts.markdown: In plane geometry each figure is restricted so that all of its parts lie in the same plane. Such figures are called *two-dimensional figures*.
excerpts.why: Gives the learner the defining restriction that separates plane figures from solid ones.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: A figure, all parts of which lie in one straight line, is a \emph{one-dimensional figure}, while a point is of zero dimensions.
excerpts.markdown: A figure, all parts of which lie in one straight line, is a *one-dimensional figure*, while a point is of zero dimensions.
excerpts.why: Places the line and the point on the same ladder of dimensions as plane and solid figures.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: In plane geometry, two lines which do not meet are parallel, while in solid geometry, two lines which do not meet need not be parallel. That is, they may not be in the same plane. Lines which are not parallel and do not meet are called \emph{skew} lines.
excerpts.markdown: In plane geometry, two lines which do not meet are parallel, while in solid geometry, two lines which do not meet need not be parallel. That is, they may not be in the same plane. Lines which are not parallel and do not meet are called *skew* lines.
excerpts.why: Shows a learner why a fact that is true in the plane fails in space, and names the new case.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: In plane geometry, ``the locus of all points at a given distance from a given point'' is a circle, while in solid geometry this locus is a sphere.
excerpts.markdown: In plane geometry, “the locus of all points at a given distance from a given point” is a circle, while in solid geometry this locus is a sphere.
excerpts.why: A short contrast that lets a learner see how the same definition of locus changes its shape when a dimension is added.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)

excerpts.markdown: If all parts of the figure are not required to lie in one plane, the theorem just quoted is far from true.
excerpts.why: Warns the learner that a plane theorem cannot be carried into space without checking its hypothesis.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: A plane is designated by a single letter in it, by two letters at opposite corners of the parallelogram representing it, or by any three letters in it but not in the same straight line.
excerpts.markdown: A plane is designated by a single letter in it, by two letters at opposite corners of the parallelogram representing it, or by any three letters in it but not in the same straight line.
excerpts.why: Gives the three standard ways to name a plane, which the learner will use throughout the book.

excerpts.markdown: The area of a circle is one half the circumference times the radius, or in symbols:

excerpts.latex: Through a point not on a given line only one straight line can be drawn parallel to that line.
excerpts.markdown: Through a point not on a given line only one straight line can be drawn parallel to that line.
excerpts.why: States the parallel postulate that plane geometry rests on, the premise the space results later qualify.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: If a line or a plane contains a point, the point is said to be \emph{on} the line or \emph{in} the plane and the line or plane is said to pass \emph{through} the point.
excerpts.markdown: If a line or a plane contains a point, the point is said to be *on* the line or *in* the plane and the line or plane is said to pass *through* the point.
excerpts.why: It fixes the basic vocabulary of 'on', 'in' and 'through' that every later figure relies on.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: While two points determine a straight line it is obvious that two points do not determine a plane.
excerpts.markdown: While two points determine a straight line it is obvious that two points do not determine a plane.
excerpts.why: It shows a learner why three points, not two, are needed to fix a plane.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: We, therefore, say that three non-collinear points determine a plane, while any number of collinear points fail to determine a plane.
excerpts.markdown: We, therefore, say that three non-collinear points determine a plane, while any number of collinear points fail to determine a plane.
excerpts.why: It states the rule for when points fix a plane, in the form a student can apply directly.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)

excerpts.markdown: In the figure, $PA$ is perpendicular to the plane $M$ and $QA$ is oblique to it.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
excerpts.latex: The perpendicular is the shortest distance from a point to a plane.
excerpts.markdown: The perpendicular is the shortest distance from a point to a plane.
excerpts.why: It explains why the distance from a point to a plane is measured along the perpendicular.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)

excerpts.markdown: Note that the four vertices of a quadrilateral in space do not necessarily all lie in the same plane.
excerpts.why: It warns learners not to assume that four points in space are coplanar.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)

excerpts.markdown: Any line, as $l_1$, in either of two parallel planes, $M$ and $N$, is parallel to the other plane.
excerpts.why: It links parallel planes to lines parallel to a plane, which is how the parallel theorems are later used.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)

excerpts.markdown: If two straight lines are cut by three parallel planes, the intercepted segments on one line are proportional to the corresponding segments on the other.

excerpts.markdown: Two half-planes meeting in a common edge form a *dihedral angle*.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)

excerpts.markdown: point on a plane is the foot of the perpendicular from the point to the plane.

excerpts.markdown: The acute angle formed by a straight line with its own projection on a plane is the least angle which it makes with any line in that plane.
excerpts.why: A vivid minimum property that explains why the angle between a line and a plane is defined through its projection.

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)

excerpts.edition: Allyn and Bacon, revised ed., 1919 (edition to be confirmed from the copy)
